newsitem.title: USA: Iraq crisis impact on U.S. Treasuries seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Iraq crisis impact on U.S. Treasuries seen limited.

text.p: A U.S. air strike against Iraq is likely to have a limited impact on the U.S. Treasury market as players are more likely to focus on the country's domestic economic outlook, analysts said.
"It's a short-term reaction," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at BT Securities Inc.
"The dominant thing this week is going to be what the economic numbers' implications are for Federal Reserve policy," he added.

The United States fired 27 cruise missiles at targets in sourthern Iraq Tuesday in response to Iraqi strikes on Kurds in the north. It was one of the biggest military attacks against Iraq since the Gulf War.

The crisis renewed tension in the Middle East, sent oil prices on a roller-coaster ride, bolstered the U.S. dollar and cast a shadow on the future of oil-for-food negotiations between the United Nations and Iraq.

Analysts said the fixed-income market might experience some short-term flight-to-quality buying in the short-end of the yield curve as some players may be willing to dock at the U.S. Treasury's safe-haven during the Iraq crisis.
But with the specter of an interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve still haunting the market, pundits said any buying of Treasury securities will be short-lived.
"The Iraq thing is temporary ... it's likely to be overshadowed by the fears of strong numbers this week and Fed tightening," Feinman said.

On Tuesday, the Treasury market was rattled early by an article in the Wall Street Journal saying the Fed is leaning toward a 50 basis-point interst rate hike if the economy does not show clear signs of slowing soon.
The Journal said the central bank could act as soon as its next policy meeting on September 24, after analyzing a slew of key employment and inflation data due before then.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January, when it cut the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current target of 5.25 percent.
Some pundits, however, expressed concerns about possible higher inflation if the crisis in Iraq lasts long enough and keeps oil prices high for the next few months.
The new complications in the oil-for-food talks between the United Nations and Iraq were seen as another factor putting longer-term upward pressure on oil prices.
"The markets had been hoping to see some Iraqi oil sooner or later ... I think there is that pressure on inflation," said Dana Johnson, head of market analysis at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
Analysts also said prolonged higher energy prices may force individuals to curb discretionary spending and, as a result, contribute to a possible economic slowdown.
"Basically what this (higher oil price) does is that it drains funds away from discretionary purchases," said Lacy Hunt, chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

By late morning, the 6-3/4-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 3/32 at 95-11/32. It pared sharp earlier losses after the NAPM report was released. Its yield was at 7.13 percent, down from 7.18 percent scored earlier.
The U.S. dollar was trading at 1.4838 against the mark and 109.25 against the yen.

Crude oil prices jumped overnight and early on Tuesday to near post Gulf War highs seen last winter, then fell back from their opening highs. NYMEX October crude stood 85 cents per at $23.10 a barrel after jumping as high as $24.25 shortly after the open. The high for benchmark Texas crude oil futures at the New York Mercantile Exchange was $24.25 a barrel, compared to a five-year high of $25.70 seen in April.

The market had a taste of the data on Tuesday, when the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said its August index rose to 52.6 from 50.2 in July. The number was mostly in line with market expectations.
Analysts said the focus is now likely to move to the key August employment report, due out on Friday, September 6.
"The market is now likely to settle a little and wait for the payrolls report," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "That is going to be a make-it-or-break-it number," he added.
